speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the avowed objective of Soviet communism is world domination. The Soviet bureaucracy does not care how long it takes or what means it uses to achieve that end. One tactic is fifth column activities. For instance, while the Soviets have been testing and piling up missiles, their fifth columns have been hypocritically and cleverly inducing as many people as possible in the NATO countries to protest the building and testing of missiles. People sincerely interested in peace have been cleverly induced into supporting this Soviet planned unilateral disarmament.
The Soviets have tripled the number of missiles that NATO countries possess, and have been testing and testing, until now their aim is 90 per cent improved over what it was two years ago. Their accuracy was tested when the Korean passenger plane was destroyed with one of their missiles and 269 innocent people, including ten Canadians, were murdered.
Yes, let us work for peace. Let us do everything possible to avoid a nuclear war, but let us be realistic. Canadians do not want a nuclear conflict. Canadians do want a world-wide reduction of nuclear armaments, a reduction that will apply to all nations and one that will be balanced, mutual, and verifiable.

subsubtopic: EROSION OF ENGLISH LANGUAGE RIGHTS IN PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 was extremely pleased yesterday with the readiness of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to meet with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) and the Leader of the NDP to prepare an all-Party resolution requesting the Legislature of Manitoba to entrench official bilingualism in that Province.
I fully support that initiative and hope that it proceeds quickly. On the other hand, I would like to remind the House that minority language rights are still threatened and under attack in other Provinces in this country.
In Quebec, my Province, the present government will not agree to entrench rights, especially the opting in to Section 23(l)(a) regarding linguistic minority education, which is in the Constitution Act of 1981. Over the years this same government has continually eroded minority language rights in that Province. Let us move ahead in Manitoba, but let us not forget that minority language groups in other Provinces have problems as well, and give them some consideration too.

subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF INDUSTRY IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canadian farmers face extinction. B.C. newspapers have headlined the distressed condition of agriculture in that Province. A thousand Okanagan fruit growers have demonstrated their frustration by rallying with hundreds of tractors, clogging highways on Labour Day.
The cry at the farmers' rally, repeated by the B.C. Minister of Agriculture, seeks imposition of temporary tariffs on imported fruits and vegetables when there is a domestic surplus. The most obvious response thus far from Canada is in a notice that Okanagan farm organizations have been charged under the Federal Combines Investigation Act. This extremely questionable action imposes an additional financial burden on farmers facing personal ruin.
Underlining the crisis, the area August jobless rate reached 14.2 per cent, up from 11.7 per cent a year ago. With unfair foreign competition threatening the demise of the last remaining fruit canning plant in the Okanagan, and with agriculture in disarray, this statistic can only worsen unless immediate action is taken.
Farmers are perplexed to read in their newspapers headlines such as "Auto import curbs hit local dealers". These farmers are simply asking the Government of Canada for treatment equitable to that provided auto and textile workers. They demand that government commit itself to the survival of agriculture, and act in their defence.
September 14, 1983

subtopic: POSITION OF PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY ON WESTERN GRAIN TRANSPORTATION ACT
POSITION OF PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY ON WESTERN GRAIN TRANSPORTATION ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is a particularly iniquitous piece of legislation being considered by a committee of this House, namely, the proposed Bill that will bring about, if passed, changes to the Crow rate. Up to this point the Conservative Party of Canada has been prepared to accept the principle of changes in the Crow rate, something that the New Democratic Party has consistently opposed.
It was remarkably refreshing to learn last night that once again the Conservatives have done a 180 degree reversal in policy and are now prepared, for at least three years, to leave the Crow rate as it is. We hope that after three years passes they will make another three years' extension. We will remain consistent in that position on that issue.
Now that they have made this change, we would like them to support the other arguments of the NDP on this Bill, namely, to split it up into three sections. One dealing with rates-let us get rid of that. The second is on the important question of upgrading rail and port facilities. We should proceed with that immediately. The next portion concerns the resolution of the ownership of an important 50,000 acres of coal land that lie in British Columbia. We in this Party say that that land should go to British Columbia, and we want Tory support on that as well.

subsubtopic: CROWSNEST PASS RATE-POSITION OF THE PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yesterday evening, the Progressive Conservative Party made another about-face on its position on the Crow's Nest Pass rate. On May 12, 1983, the Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) and Progressive Conservative critic for transport said, among other things, that the members of his Party had always taken the position that improvements to the existing statutory rate should be made and that he realized something had to be done to improve the situation. In the same statement on May 12, he also said that most producers were prepared to pay more than the statutory freight rate. Finally, he made a proposal that farmers should be allowed to decide whether payment should go to the railroads or to themselves. Yesterday evening, however, the same Member for Vegreville, speaking on behalf of the Progressive Conservative Party, made a proposal supporting a return to the status quo. This is contrary to what I read
in a letter the New Leader of the Progressive Party sent me in July, in which he supported the position taken by the Member for Vegreville on May 12, 1983, in this House.
In June 1983, in Terre de chez nous, Mario Dumais wrote an editorial under the following headline:
"One party, three policies".
Madam Speaker, from now on, we should say: One party, four policies!"

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: LACK OF NEWFOUNDLAND REPRESENTATION IN CABINET
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to express on behalf of the people of Newfoundland our profound sense of outrage over the events that have transpired since the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) was so shoddily fired from his post as Newfoundland's representative in the Cabinet. Arising out of the statement in the House by the Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons) on September 12, and the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) incredible admission in the House yesterday, we now know that the Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's was appointed to the Cabinet without the normal security check.
The Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), prior to making appointments to his Cabinet, submitted a list to the RCMP and the Department of National Revenue. It was only after clearance by these two agencies that appointments were made. That such a practice was not followed in the case of the Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's is, to put it mildly, incredible.
However, the result of this "Mickey Mouse" performance is that Newfoundland is not represented in Cabinet at a most critical time in its history. The fishing industry is in a state of bankruptcy and chaos and talks on the offshore have broken down. These problems are exacerbated by the fact that Newfoundland officially has one in five unemployed, the highest unemployment rate by far of any province.
This is a scandalous and unacceptable situation for which the Prime Minister and his colleagues stand condemned, not only by the people of Newfoundland but by the people of Canada.

subsubtopic: DELAY IN DELIVERY OF PENSION CHEQUES TO WESTERN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker,
I would like to alert Members of Parliament to a very serious example of blatant discrimination that occurs against western
September 14, 1983

Canadians, more specifically against war veterans and their families who live in certain areas of western Canada.
Many war veterans and their families depend upon the War Veterans Allowance, disability pensions, and widows' pensions to meet mortgage, utility and other financial obligations. However, in areas of western Canada these cheques regularly arrive late. In most parts of Canada war veterans and their families receive their federal cheques within two or three days of mailing, yet in certain parts of western Canada the mails result in delays of up to one week for hundreds of veterans and their families. The anxiety, frustration, and in some instances fear that result from these repeatedly late cheques are both unnecessary and unacceptable.
These veterans were prepared to die for our country, and many have suffered for many years as a result of their service. These veterans and their families deserve better recognition and treatment. I urge the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Bennett) to end this act of blatant discrimination, and I encourage all Members of the House of Commons to bring pressure on the Minister and his Department to right this very serious wrong which is being perpetrated against Canadian war veterans who have made their homes in western Canada.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CANADA HERITAGE DAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in 1974 on the first Monday in August, the Hon. Horst Schmid, then Minister of Culture in the Alberta Government, officially proclaimed the first Heritage Day in Alberta.
This multicultural event has exploded in Alberta as a day and weekend of celebration of the music, the dancing, the dress, and the food of the various ethnic groups which now form the Alberta society.
This year in Edmonton alone nearly 500,000 people attended the two day heritage festival held at Hawrelak Park to enjoy the music, dance, costumes, and food of the 52 ethnic groups that participated. It was a wonderful expression of the multicultural roots and customs of Canada's diversified peoples and their unique Canadianism.
The time has now come to make the heritage festival a national event. Indeed, it is my intention to bring forth before Parliament a Private Member's Bill to declare the first Monday in August an official national holiday designated as Canada Heritage Day.

that Bill C-407, an Act to amend the Criminal Code (cruelty to animals), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to stand at last and say a few words about this Bill to the House. It is one that had its first reading over three years ago on May 2, 1980, and I hope that it is not a measure of the esteem that the House has for our friends from the animal kingdom that it has taken over three years to arrive at this debate.
I should say at the outset, Mr. Speaker, that this Bill does not touch upon laboratory testing or experimentation with animals. Great advances have been made in medical research through the controlled laboratory testing of and experiments on animals. This important aspect of the situation was discussed in some detail this week by a well-known columnist, none other than Ann Landers. In reference to the alleged cruelty to animals in research laboratories, that well-known columnist observed, probably speaking about the United States of America, that 13 million dogs and cats alone were destroyed in shelters in that country last year because no one wanted them. As well, Mr. Speaker, she pointed out that:
Animal experimentation made it possible to immunize millions of children, all over the world, against polio, diphtheria, mumps, measles, hepatitis, etc. Add to that list every person who receives an antibiotic to fight infection, insulin for diabetes, anti-inflammatory agents for arthritis, chemotherapy for cancer, medication to control hypertension and drugs for the treatment of mental illness.
Every person who has undergone the replacement of-a joint, or the reattachment of a severed finger or limb, kidney dialysis, heart surgery or organ transplantation owes a debt to animal experimentation.
Those procedures are carried out under controlled circumstances, and I point out again that they are not the subject of the debate today. We should recognize that the alternative to using animals in laboratories is of course the use of humans, which use I have not heard advocated. 1 quote now from the Bill:
The purpose of this Bill is to enlarge the scope of subsection 402(1) of the Criminal Code prohibiting cruelty to animals. This is done in three ways; first, it expands the application of these provisions to anyone who causes wilful or negligent injury to an animal. Second, it provides that an owner cannot permit negligent or wilful damage to an animal or bird and, third, it imposes a duty on the part of owners and those in control of animals to provide them with suitable maintenance.
Cruelty to Animals
This will mean that owners and others who are keeping animals will have to provide a standard of care such that the animals' health cannot be impaired by the actions of that person or of strangers. Moreover, this expansion of the subsection will make it more enforceable as it will clearly encompass negligent as well as wilful behaviour in regard to the care of animals or birds.
Now, the present Section 402(1) of the Criminal Code does list a number of offences, but some of the definitions are too skimpy. In order to detail the proposed changes, I would like to read the first three paragraphs of Subsection 402(1), which read as follows:
Everyone commits an offence who
(a)	wilfully causes or, being the owner, wilfully permits to be caused unnecessary pain, suffering or injury to an animal or bird,
(b)	by wilful neglect causes damage or injury to animals or birds while they are being driven or conveyed,
(c)	being the owner or the person having the custody or control of a domestic animal or bird or an animal or bird wild by nature that is in captivity, abandons it in distress or wilfully neglects or fails to provide suitable and adequate food, water, shelter and care for it.
Those are the first three paragraphs, Mr. Speaker, of Subsection (1) of Section 402.
The proposal that I make in Bill C-407 is a very simple one and it is that those three paragraphs be repealed and be substituted by three subsections which would read as follows:
(a)	wilfully or negligently causes unnecessary hardship, privation, suffering or injury to any animal or bird,
(b)	being the owner or a person having custody or control of any animal or bird, wilfully or negligently permits unnecessary hardship, privation, suffering or injury to be caused to such animal or bird,
(c)	being the owner or a person having custody or control of any animal or bird, abandons it in distress or wilfully or negligently fails to provide suitable and adequate food, water, shelter and care for it.
To summarize, Mr. Speaker, the comparisons are that the old Code refers to pain, suffering or injury, whereas the clause I am proposing uses the terminology "hardship, privation, suffering or injury". After all, pain is a matter of subjective definition and hardship and privation would extend that definition.
The word "negligently" has been added in all three paragraphs because wilful action was the only provision made in the old wording. The original provision referred to wilful neglect while being driven or conveyed. That is now eliminated because it is included in the new definition of hardship, privation, suffering or injury.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the new wording expands the definition of animal or bird by the use of the word "any". This means that now the animal concerned does not have to be a domestic or wild animal but would be any animal or bird.
1 ask the support of the House for this Bill which will be to the benefit of our furred and feathered friends. I hope all Members of the House will feel as charitably about this as I do.

Mr. Speaker, I think we all appreciate the concern of the Hon. Member for

September 14, 1983
Cruelty to Animals
Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Clarke) in bringing this Bill forward, and I should like to make a few comments on it.
The Bill under consideration proposes to make minor amendments to the Criminal Code provisions dealing with cruelty to animals. The proposal's key feature is to make a negligent act of cruelty to an animal a criminal offence. Very few negligent acts with respect to human beings are governed by the criminal law, so I do not see why we should afford more protection to animals than we do to people.
A criminal offence generally requires an actus reus and a mens rea. The act must be committed plus the person committing the act must have the required intention. Where a person does not intend the consequences of his act or does not have the necessary mental state to understand that the act is wrong, he is generally not punished by the criminal law. There are few exceptions to this rule.
The Criminal Code currently defines criminal negligence in Section 202(1). The Section states:
Everyone is criminally negligent who
(a)	in doing anything, or
(b)	in omitting to do anything that it is his duty to do,
shows wanton or reckless disregard for the lives or safety of other persons.
Subsection 202(2) adds:
For the purposes of this section, "duty" means a duty imposed by law.
This same type of recklessness is contemplated by Section 402 dealing with cruelty to animals due to the application of Section 386.
Section 386(1) provides:
Everyone who causes the occurrence of an event by doing an act or by omitting to do an act that it is his duty to do, knowing that the act or omission will probably cause the occurrence of the event and being reckless whether the event occurs or not, shall be deemed, for the purposes of this Part, wilfully to have caused the occurrence of the event.
If Section 402 is read completely and in the context of Part IX of the Code, it is apparent that advertent negligence or recklessness is already included. Further, by the operation of Subsections 402(3) and 386(1), proof of simple negligence is, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, proof of advertent negligence or recklessness.
Subsection 402(3) states:
-evidence that a person failed to exercise reasonable care or supervision of an animal or bird thereby causing it pain, suffering, damage or injury is, in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, proof that such pain, suffering, damage or injury was caused or was permitted to be caused wilfully or was caused by wilful neglect, as the case may be.
Since negligence means the failure to exercise reasonable care, the current Subsection 402(3) would appear to accomplish the intended purpose of the proposed amendment.
The Hon. Member has mentioned that the Government's policy with respect to criminal law is to reserve its use for conduct for which other means of control are inadequate and inappropriate. The Provinces have enacted legislation with respect to cruelty to animals which focuses on protection and rehabilitation of the animal rather than punishment of the owner or custodian.
The Provinces have also enacted legislation imposing certain standards of care where animals are used for research.
The current Criminal Code provisions are more than adequate to deter and punish those who deliberately or recklessly harm animals. There is no need for amendment. The proposed amendments add little to the current law.
May I also point out that it is premature to consider any amendments to the Criminal Code at this time, especially unnecessary amendments. The Members of the House of Commons are well aware that the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) is currently involved in a fundamental and comprehensive review of the Criminal Code, in the course of which Section 402 will be considered. The Criminal Code was originally enacted in 1892, and since that date there have been a continuous series of patchwork amendments. The criminal law review is aimed at the enactment of a modern, responsible and effective criminal law for Canada based on consistent and fundamental principles. This review has been undertaken in co-operation with the Ministry of the Solicitor General and in close consultation with the Provinces. The recommendations of the Law Reform Commission of Canada will be reviewed and a detailed examination of all substantive and procedural aspects of Canadian criminal law will be conducted.
Each section of the present Criminal Code will be examined in light of the principles stated in the Criminal Law in Canadian Society which were discussed by the Hon. Member. The sections will also be reviewed with regard to the numerous amendments that have been proposed but not adopted and their intended purpose.
The consideration of minor amendments to seldom used sections at this time is likely to lead to more patchwork legislation. The consideration of Section 402 will be thoroughly dealt with by the House when undertaking its analysis of proposed amendments resulting from the criminal law review process. I would therefore suggest that the proposed amendments be dealt with at that time.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to support the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Clarke) who presented Bill C-407. I find it somewhat refreshing that after days, weeks, and months of debate on important economic issues, we set aside time for topics that some people may consider frivolous. The Bill before us shows some sensitivity for living creatures other than human beings.
As Parliamentarians we have shown our concern for a quality environment in various pieces of legislation that we have debated over the years. These indicate a genuine interest in the preservation of a quality environment.
There have also been some very strong statements on human rights from both sides of the House, so I find it refreshing that today we are attempting to make changes to the Criminal Code that would provide greater safety and better protection for the animal and bird kingdoms.
I want to use this occasion to extend this debate into an area that goes a bit beyond the intent of the Bill in some respects,
September 14, 1983

and that is the matter of laboratory testing and experimentation and the use of animals for this purpose. I think, perhaps, the most offending industry in this area would be the cosmetic industry. 1 was alerted, and I assume all Members of Parliament have been alerted many, many times, to what many people feel is a questionable use of animals in the testing of items such as cosmetics and toothpaste. 1 flag the attention of Parliament by mention of the Draize test, which is a test used on rabbits, animals which have no tear ducts. Perfumes of various kinds and various kinds of cosmetics are squirted in the eyes of rabbits to see the reaction over a period of time. I suppose this is to see what would happen if, for instance, Chanel No. 5 was squirted in someone's eyes, what they could expect in terms of some physiological reaction.
I simply use this, Mr. Speaker, as as example of the kind of tests through which we put various kinds of animals in our experimentation with all sorts of technologies and substances and the like. I would like to draw the attention of Parliament to the efforts of a particular group called, "The International Wildlife Protection Association". This is an international organization based here in Canada which takes this argument a little further, saying that if Parliamentarians are indeed concerned about protecting animals and birds from neglect, from various sorts of hardships, then perhaps we should give some attention to wildlife in that same vein. The International Wildlife Protection Association has for years raised the question with respect to the killing of wild animals for pleasure, such as trophy hunting, and it has written to Members of Parliament and has asked us on many occasions to question that kind of behaviour in a country such as ours.
I remember very distinctly, as a young man growing up in the Kamloops area as a hunter at the time, taking advantage of the abundance of wildlife in our area. We would go out hunting in the evenings and normally have occasion to encounter many, many deer. Yet as the years pass there are fewer and fewer wildlife of all sorts to be seen. I do not believe there is any question but that in many cases indiscriminate hunting practices have resulted in the reduction in many of our wildlife species. 1 simply flag this issue on their behalf for Parliamentarians, that indeed if we are as serious as this Bill would indicate about domestic animals and their protection, we should give that same consideration to wild animals and question the matter of hunting and killing of wild animals for pleasure only. 1 am not questioning the concept of taking the lives of wild animals for food by those who need it and use it in their traditional lifestyle, but I do want to question the matter of the killing of wild animals for pleasure, particularly as emphasized by the trophy hunter.
I would also like to mention, Mr. Speaker, that this Bill touches on a very critical question for those who are interested in the animal world and the need for their protection. There is one other aspect of this issue having to do with kangaroos. I know that kangaroos are not usually a topic we get into here in Canada, but we do import kangaroo products into our country, both in terms of hides and meat, as well as various decorations
Cruelty to Animals
made, presumably, from kangaroo feet and ears, and the like. In Australia three million kangaroos are killed annually, legally. In other words, they are killed by using proper hunting techniques and in appropriate seasons. What I would like to flag, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that three million kangaroos are killed illegally in Australia and, to a large extent, I believe that Canada is a recipient of this illegal trade, the hides and paraphernalia associated with the killing of kangaroos.
I applaud the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra for bringing this Bill forward. I support it, together with my colleagues, and will say that perhaps this is just the beginning of a much longer debate around the topic of protecting both domestic and wild animals and birds.

Mr. Speaker,
I think the House owes a debt of gratitude to the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) for bringing this matter to our attention. I would like to think that there is a means whereby we could have this Bill, which some might consider defective in certain respects or with certain shortfalls, referred to an appropriate committee for study, improvement and adoption.
I was really quite astounded, Mr. Speaker, I did not believe my ears at first, when I heard the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae) say that it was "inappropriate"- I believe that was the word he used-for Members of Parliament to bring forward proposals to amend the Criminal Code at this particular stage because, he went on, the Government was already revising the Criminal Code. Where else, Mr. Speaker, from which quarter, should proposals to amend the Criminal Code come if not from this House?
The Law Commission, 1 agree, should certainly make its proposals. However, to suggest that Members of Parliament should be muzzled or be told to sit down and be quiet because the Government is coming forward with a complete revision of the Criminal Code is, to my way of thinking, just typical of the arrogance of this Government! 1 listened in disbelief that anyone in this House would suggest that we should not bring forward matters of concern to us.
The date on this particular Bill is May 2, 1980. This Bill is three years old. How long has the Criminal Code been under revision? 1 venture to say it has been under revision for a long time, and if the comments made during this debate cannot contribute to the revision of the Criminal Code, Mr. Speaker, we are wasting our time here and we are receiving messages from the other side of the House that that is exactly what we are doing. This House has no relevance in the eyes of the Government, otherwise an Hon. Member would not stand up and read such a speech, which was prepared for him-because I cannot believe that that particular Member would have written that speech himself, honourable Member that he is. 1 cannot believe that he would put those words together in his own mind. It must have come from some official in the Public Service who wanted that message put across, "Don't worry us. We've got the Criminal Code under control. Now, don't you upset the Criminal Code cart because we are busy with it and

we will come up with the appropriate amendments when the time comes. You just sit back and think about something else."
"We will do what is good for you."

That is right. I did mention some of the shortcomings of this particular Bill. None of us are particularly keen, I am sure, about reptiles. There may be some who like lizards, some who like boa constrictors, and that kind of thing. However, 1 believe we should broaden the meaning of term "animal", because a reptile is not an animal according to the proper dictionary definition. We should, perhaps, broaden the meaning because 1 am sure this is what the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra had in mind. This is a humanitarian Bill for the animal world. I suppose that is about the best way I can put it at the moment. 1 am sure the Hon. Member would want the provision he is trying to have included in the law cover reptiles as well as birds and animals.
I think it is an excellent notion to include those who, through negligence, cause harm to animals, birds or reptiles. We have no provision within the rules, as I understand them, for proposing amendments to these Bills but 1 do feel that if it could be taken to committee, that particular amendment might be added.
1 was very pleased to hear the comments of the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). He revealed a completely new aspect of his attitude towards the living creatures of this world in his comments just a few minutes ago. I was delighted that he should think of those frightful experiments which are carried out on wild animals by the cosmetic profession.
1 cannot let this occasion pass, Mr. Speaker, without making some comments about killer whales. There is a school of do-gooders, I guess you call them, who feel that no animal should be kept in captivity. No animal should be subjected to the spectacles that we all enjoy such as circuses. We enjoy watching trained horses, trained bears, and we enjoy learning about killer whales. They are amazing animals, Mr. Speaker, and we had one out in Victoria which suffered a fate too horrible to mention in ordinary circumstances, but 1 feel compelled to mention it now.
Some of these do-gooders, to the best of my knowledge, tried to release that killer whale from its pool in Sealand in Victoria. They went down as divers to cut the wires at the bottom of the pool so this killer whale could gain his freedom in the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Something seemed to have disturbed them or they did not get the dimensions of the killer whale right. The killer whale went down, nosed around, got his head caught in the wire and was unable to come up to the surface to breathe. That whale drowned because of the deliberate act of some vandals who claim to be concerned about the welfare of wild animals.
How can we know how to treat wild animals if we cannot study them and see what they can do in performances and how grateful they are for the care that is given to them? That there
should be no wild animals in captivity is a nonsensical notion. They have to be properly cared for, and no zoo that I know of would dare open to the public without proper zoologists and people trained in animal care. We have a very special team of people at Sealand in Victoria who know how to deal with these sea mammals, and I cannot express too deeply the horror that struck me when I heard that that animal had been drowned. There was this great creature to which 1 had the good fortune to actually talk and to stroke and touch, it came up to see me when 1 was down by the side of the pool. It was a magnificent feeling, and some vandals had the audacity to cause that animal to drown.
Attempts are being made to restore that show at Sealand in Victoria and there has been a great furor about people getting killer whales from somewhere else and bringing them to Victoria.
1 see the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Masters) is here now. I hope he is blushing for having suggested that we should not even discuss amendments to the Criminal Code.
To come back to the killer whales, 1 do feel that when care and proper treatment of these wild animals is fully understood, and licensed if necessary, and registered trainers and caretakers of these animals are in place, then it is no offence whatsoever and should not be an offence to have them in captivity.
So, Mr. Speaker, if there is any possibility of making a motion on this particular Bill, with its strengths and defects, I would move, if 1 can without being out of order, that the subject matter of this Bill be referred to an appropriate committee of the House. If so, I so move.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, welcome this opportunity to speak on Bill C-407, a Private Members' Bill put forward by the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Clarke). The intent of the Bill is most admirable. No one can argue against the need to protect animals from unnecessary suffering, and I congratulate the Hon. Member for raising this issue in the House.
1 was particularly concerned that this was another attempt to downgrade and be critical of the work done on animals in experimental laboratories, and I called the Member to ask his feelings on this. I was particularly pleased to hear from him by telephone and in his remarks here today that he appreciated the role animals play in medical research and the contribution
September 14, 1983

they make to a better understanding of medical and surgical problems and the opportunities they give to make very positive contributions to our health and ability to fight disease. 1 can give personal assurance of that having taken part in a great deal of basic research work done on cardiac surgery at the Hospital for Sick Children. I worked there with Doctor William Mustard. A great deal of the duties of a resident is to carry out the various operative procedures on these animals, and I can assure you that the greater part of a resident's life at that time was to provide intensive care for these animals, and throughout the succeeding days after the operation these animals received the very best, most intensive and skilful care. This was to ensure that they would survive and be comfortable and, indeed, to show the efficacy of a number of these operative procedures which have now become standard and which contribute immensely to the welfare of many young patients, changing that aspect of surgery. I therefore congratulate the Hon. Member, the proposer of the Bill, for having had foresight and understanding as far as that particular role is concerned.
The Bill proposes to amend the Criminal Code provisions with respect to cruelty to animals, namely, Subsection 402. The alleged purpose of the amendments is to enlarge the scope of Subsection 402(1) by expanding its application to anyone who causes wilful or negligent injury to animals or birds. I am stressing "wilful or negligent". The amendments also provide that an owner cannot permit wilful or negligent damage to an animal or bird, and imposes a duty on owners or those having care or control of animals to provide them with suitable and adequate food, water, shelter and care.
In my own reading and study of the Bill as it was presented, I thoroughly agreed with the spirit that it represented. However, in studying the Bill with the help of the legal experts of the Department of Justice, I found that the legal implications placed certain problem before me. At the moment, taking into consideration the thoughts expressed by lawyers, I find that the amendments, in comparison with the present Criminal Code, should be considered unnecessary.
A close reading of the current Criminal Code provisions indicates that the type of conduct the Bill seeks to make criminal is already prohibited. For example, subsection 402(3) states that with respect to the present paragraphs, Subsection 402(l)(a) and Subsection 402(l)(b), "evidence that a person failed to exercise reasonable care or supervision of an animal or bird thereby causing it pain, suffering, damage or injury is, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, proof that such pain, suffering, damage or injury was caused or was permitted to be caused wilfully or was caused by wilful neglect, as the case may be". Negligence is the failure to exercise reasonable care. Thus, adding the words "negligently causes" to Subsection 402(1) would be redundant.
Although Section 402 currently uses the word "wilful", the word has a special meaning and is not limited to intentional acts. Section 402 is located in Part IX of the Criminal Code.
Cruelty to Animals
Section 386, also in Part IX, provides that for the purposes of this Part of the Code, certain types of conduct are deemed to be "wilful". The Section provides that "everyone who causes the occurence of an event by doing an act or by omitting to do an act that it is his duty to do, knowing that the act or omission will probably cause the occurence of the event and being reckless whether the event occurs or not, shall be deemed, for the purposes of this Part, wilfully to have caused the occurrence of the event". Thus, recklessness is covered by the provision and "recklessness" means advertent negligence.
Very few crimes carry responsibility for simple or civil negligence. It is not clear what type of negligence is being proposed. Again, from a legal interpretation and legal study, one finds that the Criminal Code defines "criminal negligence" in Section 202 as follows: "(1) everyone is criminally negligent who (a) in doing anything or (b) in omitting to do anything that it is his duty to do, shows wanton or reckless disregard for the lives or safety of other persons". Subsection 202(2) states: "for the purposes of this Section, "duty" means a duty imposed by law". This duty must arise by virtue of a statute or a common law. There is no reason to impose a higher standard of care for animals than for human beings. Nevertheless, whether the negligence sought to be made criminal by the proposed amendments is advertent negligence, that is, recklessness, or simple inadvertent negligence, both types of conduct are already adequately covered by Sub-sections 386(1) and 402(3).
The proposed amendment also seeks to change the wording of paragraph 402(1 )(a) from "unnecessary pain, suffering or injury" to "unnecessary hardship, privation, suffering or injury". It is impossible to determine what constitutes "hardship" for an animal by any objective standard. Of more importance, however, is that "privation" is defined in the Oxford dictionary as "want of the comforts or necessaries of life". How can we determine what the "comforts of life" are for an animal, as opposed to "necessaries"? There is no objective test.
Animals, by their very nature, can take care of themselves if left alone. We have raised the standard of life for animals by bringing them into our homes, feeding them, grooming them and taking them on family vacations. It cannot be said that a farmer who lets his dogs and cats run free and sleep outside is cruel. Animals and birds are equipped to provide themselves with the necessaries of life. People cannot be said to be negligent if they fail to do so. Furthermore, upon whom is the duty to provide the necessaries of life to animals imposed? Wild animals and stray domestic animals have no owner or custodian to be responsible for them. The question raised is: "Am I my neighbour's dogkeeper?"
Furthermore, do we wish to make it a crime punishable by a maximum fine of, say, $500 and/or six months' imprisonment for failing to provide "comforts" to an animal as opposed to "necessaries"? Not even in respect of humans is it a criminal offence to fail to provide the comforts of life. Under Section 197 of the Criminal Code, it is only an offence not to provide the "necessaries of life."

September 14, 1983
Cruelty to Animals
In any event, the current wording, "pain, suffering, or injury", should encompass the type of discomfort sought to be prohibited. In addition, Paragraph 402(l)(c) states that "everyone commits an offence who, being the owner or the person having the custody or control of a domestic animal or bird or an animal or bird wild by nature that is in captivity, abandons it in distress or wilfully neglects or fails to provide suitable and adequate food, water, shelter and care for it". Thus, it is already an offence to fail to provide the necessaries of life for an animal. There is no need to impose any higher standards.
The wording of the proposed amendments is very similar to many provincial statutes dealing with cruelty to animals. The provincial statutes are designed to prevent cruelty to animals and protect and relieve animals from such cruelty. The owners or custodians of animals can be ordered to change their practices or the animals can be taken from them. The purpose is to protect the animal and not necessarily to punish the owner or custodian. For example, the Ontario Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act has as its object the prevention of cruelty to animals and their protection and relief therefrom. For the purpose of the enforcement of any law or statute in force pertaining to the welfare of or the prevention of cruelty to animals, every inspector and agent of the society or an affiliated society has the powers of a police officer. An inspector or agent of the society may obtain a warrant to search a building or place for animals in distress, or where he observes an animal in immediate distress he may enter without a warrant any premises or building or place other than a dwelling house. Other Provinces have similar legislation.
If our concern is for the animal, then the provincial provisions are sufficient. The Criminal Code should remain unchanged in focusing its concern upon the moral culpability of the actor. Therefore, the proposed amendment is considered unnecessary.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a person who has spent most of his working life concerned with the care and welfare of animals, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak in this debate. I would like to compliment the Hon. Member for bringing to the attention of the House and therefore to the attention of the Canadian people the fact that there is a sensitivity to the welfare of all animals.
I would also like to bring to the attention of the Hon. Member who proposed this Bill when he said in his opening statement that the only alternative to using animals in testing and experimentation is to use the human that this is not exactly the case. There are many alternatives now being studied which would replace animals in experimentation. I am thinking of such things as tissue culture, microbial units and biochemical test. Of course, we now have the simulator and the computer.
I would like to point out to the House that experimental institutions which perform animal experimentation and various organizations which are concerned with animal welfare are vigorously pursuing the use of these kinds of alternatives. As a person who has spent quite a bit of my life doing and supervising animal experimentation, there is nothing that I, and 1 am sure many of my colleagues, would like better than to see the day when we would not have to use animals at all for experimentation. However, until such time I think we have to look at what is available to us and, up to this moment, we must use animals because they are the only biological model which we presently have. I would like to reiterate that there is nothing I would like to see more than the time when we can completely exclude living animals from experimentation.
I would also like to bring the thought forward to the House that it is man himself who demands safety tests, which makes it necessary for us to use animals at the present time. Of course, we look to the idea of replacing this with other kinds of models in the future.
For those in the House who are not familiar with what a simulator or a computer can do, it is now quite possible by way of computer to develop a model which is completely representative of the respiratory system or cardiovascular system. Therefore, instead of having to use innumerable live animals, it is quite possible to develop a computer program which allow us to make variations in our experimental design which could be measured on this simulator. For example, it is possible for medical students today to have a computer which they can program to determine what will happen if they use a certain drug. Previously, they would have to had to use a patient and decide to inject this drug into the patient or wait until a suitable patient with that certain cardiovascular defect came into the clinic before having the opportunity to treat that patient.
September 14, 1983

Computers can now be designed to simulate that patient. If the medical student's treatment does not work and he receives a signal that the patient died, it is only the program that did not work. One can imagine the possibilities for replacing animals by experimentation by this type of computer.
I would also bring to the attention of the House the fact that we are not allowing animal welfare to fall into disrepute without some kind of surveillance or control. There are two areas with which I am concerned. One is animal experimentation. Canada has the only volunteer organization which is composed of people who are controlling animal experimentation. It is called the Canadian Council on Animal Care. A question presently being asked is whether things should be regulated by law or whether people should be educated so that they recognize their responsibilities and do not need laws to guide them. I believe that if people are properly informed and can decide on that information, it is quite often evident that the rules they establish for themselves are at an even higher level than those established by the law. When laws are made it must be kept in mind that they must be enforceable. With respect to animal welfare, a law which was passed to control how animals are treated would have to be enforceable. People would simply abide by the minimums of the law. In my experience they have said that what they are trying to do requires a much higher level than that established by the law. This is the kind of surveillance we have with the Canadian Council of Animal Care in scientific institutions in Canada. I am quite convinced that this is working and will continue to work to the betterment of animal welfare.
Of course, the second group of animals with which we are concerned are domestic animals, pets, wild animals, animals in zoos; in other words, animals in general that are not covered by the group which controls animal experimentation in scientific institutions. At this point I would like to draw the Canadian Federation of Humane Societies to the attention of the House. It is an umbrella group with which other humane society units in the country are allied. Its major concern is to look after the welfare of animals. It has a very close relationship with the federal Government when it comes to looking after animals being slaughtered, animals in transit or any animal which falls under the control of the federal Government. It is also concerned with animals in exhibitions. It is interested in animals being slaughtered, what happens to them when they are being transported to slaughter houses and at the time they are being slaughtered.
What interests me about the Canadian Federation of Humane Societies is that it has a great interest in education, an area through which sensitivity can be developed starting in elementary schools and through the secondary school system. Certainly I remember in elementary school Humane Society Day which occurred once a year. We were given buttons to wear which read, "Be kind to animals". We were given pictures of animals, and very often someone visited our school to tell students about the need to care for animals. This is the basis for the development of sensitivity. All the laws in the
Blood Samples
world will not ensure that animals are properly cared for, but if we can develop such a sensitivity in young people in the early stages, by the time they reach the point where they own animals, view animals in zoos or, if they are professionals, use animals for experimentation purposes, they will have that sensitivity and laws will not be needed to govern their activities.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POWER TO TAKE BLOOD SAMPLES

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Wenman (Fraser Valley West) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POWER TO TAKE BLOOD SAMPLES
speechtext:
that Bill C-625, an Act to amend the Criminal Code (power to take blood samples), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to allow for the testing of blood samples for blood alcohol levels in the case of motor vehicle accidents. Drivers are not now subject to blood alcohol testing when suspected of driving while impaired.
I would like to read the following excerpt from a letter of Mr. John Steward:
My son is dead! Peter Graham Steward, aged 23 years, three months and 11 days has been killed. A boy entering adult life, a boy with a blameless life, hard working, reliable and essentially good right through. This lad, my youngest son, was murdered by an unthinking and totally uncaring man, a man who had so soused himself in whisky and beer that he had shed all vestige of manhood, amounting to an uncontrolled and dangerous state of mental awareness.
The boy whom we had loved from the moment of birth, our youngest son, so full of promise and love himself for his Mum, Dad, brothers and sisters was no more, gone forever, gone to the world from which he came to us all, leaving behind broken hearts and numbed minds asking why, why? His fiancee and impending marriage plans destroyed, his brothers and sisters, hopelessly trying to find comfort in each other, Mum and Dad, with an ache that is beyond comprehension by those who have never suffered such a loss.
It continued:
The police hands are tied, the doctors under threat of prosecution, and the guilty one, a host of lawyers will defend him, and without proof, clinical proof, the murderer goes free.
The time has come that no government should tolerate such inequity in laws. Too many are dying on Canada's roads, and many are victims of protected murderers with large and terrible weapons of destruction on four wheels.
I appeal to the Government to right this appalling injustice.
The murderer in this case has continued to drive freely on our highways ever since that tragic day in 1977.

September 14, 1983
Blood Samples
I could quote figures from many jurisdictions throughout Canada, but I will just take one to indicate the volume, and scale of tragedy, sorrow, anger and pain. In the Province of British Columbia alone in 1982 there were 24,000 accidents with injury or death. There were 600 deaths and 34,000 injuries. In 20 per cent of all accidents with injury, one or more drivers were drinking. In 40 per cent of all accidents with death, one or more drivers were drinking, and 10 per cent to 20 per cent of all drivers injured in accidents had been drinking. Studies by the Attorney General's office showed that in the evenings 6 per cent of all drivers legally impaired had over .08 per cent blood alcohol levels and 6 per cent who had been drinking had between .05 per cent and .08 per cent blood alcohol levels.
When parents and families suffer such a loss, first comes the anger, then comes perhaps even revenge, but ultimately they say that above all they want justice and that anything which we enact must be enacted with that motive. They have indicated this to me, so it makes somewhat of a difference that justice be applied.
In 1980 a study of 1,500 cases involving drinking drivers showed an over-all conviction rate of 87 per cent. When blood alcohol testing was involved, 90 per cent admitted their crime and pleaded guilty. When no testing was involved, only 70 per cent pleaded guilty. We are talking about 20 per cent more people. It has been demonstrated that blood alcohol testing will, hopefully, save lives. It certainly saves time and brings these matters before our courts and through to justice.
Where does concern for this particular area start? I suppose we want to lay blame first of all. Maybe blame is where it does start. Certainly blame should first be placed on the social disease of drunken driving. Second, and equally important, there must be accountability and restitution. That should be the result and responsibility of the person who perpetrated the crime, who bent his arm one time too many.
As a result of this tragic incident, I drafted Bill C-625 before us today. I have named it the Steward amendment. I do not have a right to put a name on the Bill, but I am naming it that because it was his personal tragedy that struck me so deeply that I felt we must begin a course of action.
This is not just in Canada. It is also in the United States. President Reagan has declared war on drunken driving and has formed a presidential commission. Across Canada, citizens' groups have been provoked to action by their horror of such wanton carnage. They have been formed to lobby for such legislative changes, not just in this House of Commons, but in the Provinces across the country. One such group which many Members have heard from is Sally Gribble's MADD organization, "Mothers Against Drunk Drivers". On their behalf I presented this year a petition signed by 7,000 Canadians who want to see the law changed and see justice found in this area.
Since 1978 when the Bill in its first form was presented by me as Bill C-428, substantial and significant support has been
building for it across the country. Many organizations have expressed support in principle for this Bill. As long ago as 1978 I received letters from the Attorneys-General of British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario. Also in support have been the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police, The Canadian Medical Association, the Australian Medical Association, the Salvation Army, Casabello Wines and the Canadian Automobile Association. Since that time many other groups have begun to express their opinions. They have been expressing concern over this Bill and its ramifications. Taking compulsory blood samples from drunken drivers who kill is a legal, moral and social problem with legal, civil libertarian and medical aspects. It is not an easy problem to legislate, but there are some small steps that we can take. This Bill is one of them. The Government of Canada's avowed policy on criminal law, as stated in its recent publication "The Criminal Law in Canadian Society" embraces the following, and I quote:
The purpose of the criminal law is to contribute to the maintenance of a just, peaceful and safe society through the establishment of a system of prohibitions, sanctions and procedures to deal fairly and appropriately with culpable conduct that causes or threatens serious harm to individuals or society!
With this promise and commitment, a loophole in Canadian law exists that allows drunken drivers involved in accidents to escape detection by breathalyzer and thereby escape prosecution. Drivers often feign injury to avoid taking the breathalyzer. As the President of the Canadian Medical Association notes:
It's becoming a common dodge. People who are in the know, know that they can feign injury and avoid the test.
If they feign injury in an accident, they are sent to hospital, thereby avoiding the drunken driving breathalyzer test.
The attitude of civil libertarians to this issue is that mandatory blood tests would be a violation of individual rights. That maybe so to some small extent. However, I feel strongly that the taking of an innocent human life is a far greater violation not only of an individual right but also of the most sacred principle of natural and positive law, the right to life of that person who died as a result of the actions of another person.
Legislators and the legal profession have recognized this fact. This study, which was begun in the mid-1970s, has resulted in the Law Reform Commission publishing working paper 29, "The General Part Liabilities and Practices", which included a proposal to change the Criminal Code to create a new category of offence called criminal intoxication.
Three years ago the Conservative Government of Manitoba actually enacted such a Bill. The Social Credit Government of British Columbia has legislation due to be proclaimed October 1 to institute mandatory blood alcohol tests for suspected drunk drivers involved in accidents. The Saskatchewan Conservative Government Vehicles Act, 1983, Section 168(1), provides that a medical practitioner, registered nurse or qualified lab technician may be allowed to take a sample of blood if the police officer, on reasonable and probable grounds, believes a person had consumed alcohol or drugs and was operating a motor vehicle within the preceding two hours.
September 14, 1983

It is not just our Provinces or this country which have been acting in this sphere in the last five years. The California vehicle act, Section 13353, provides that, and I quote:
-any person who drives a motor vehicle upon a highway shall be deemed to have given his consent to a chemical test of his blood, breath or urine for the purpose of determining the alcohol content of his blood if lawfully arrested for any offence allegedly committed while the person was driving a motor vehicle under the influence of intoxicating liquor.
Some people ask about the constitutional validity. The constitutional validity of taking blood samples to determine impairment was upheld in the Constitution of the United States in the case of Schmerber v. California. In Western Australia, the Road Traffic Act, Section 66 (2), provides that a patrolman can allow a medical practitioner to take a sample of the offender's blood for analysis.
In light of recent legislation by Provinces, increased public awareness, intensified legal interest and further study, I would like to recommend that it is well past time for action by this House of Commons on this subject.
This is not new. We are not plotting new ground. We are responding to a reality of lifestyle and a reality of tragedy. As 1 mentioned, in one Province alone there have been 600 deaths, 240 related to drunken driving. What is the delay in this legislation? Since I first proposed this legislation, which has sat around for a long time, I have received a lot of constructive advice. For example, I received from Ernie Hawrish, a lawyer friend in Saskatoon in whom I have great faith, a suggestion that perhaps this Bill needs further amendment and suggestions. He says that perhaps there needs to be a section for appropriate fines and imprisonment as well as an extension of the range of persons qualified to take such tests. Others have suggested that the question of the use of the material gained in such a test as evidence needs further discussion.
It is my request to this House of Commons today that this Bill, which is an idea, be referred to the standing committee. I would like to hear testimony. Let us hear from MADD and the Stewards about the tragedy of the victims. Let us hear from those who cannot have returned what has been taken. Why would the Government not grant this? Why would the Government not want this for Canadians? This is the initiative of a Private Member but it should have been an initiative of the House of Commons of Canada. This is not a bipartisan political issue, it is a human issue. Why does the Member on the Government side who is told to respond to this matter not get on to it right now? Do not delay it three months or six months or three years or five years while people die all over our highways.
Whoever has been assigned to respond to this Bill should stand up right now. Do not talk it out. That person knows how to make a simple reference of the subject matter now. He has the necessary information. He should make this reference now. Do not talk it out. No more talk is required, only action is required. It could be your son, it could be your daughter, it could be your family, it could be you.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POWER TO TAKE BLOOD SAMPLES
speechtext: Maybe "entirely" is the last word.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POWER TO TAKE BLOOD SAMPLES
speechtext:
That would be a good word to have there. From time to time we read in the newspapers that we will be infrining upon the individual rights of the people of Canada. I stand shoulder to shoulder with Hon. Members and say, what about the rights of the victims? What about the rights of the grieving families that are left behind? What about the young lives that are snuffed out because some men and women consider it more important to drink themselves into a stupor than to care for their fellow man?

September 14, 1983
Blood Samples
The Minister has told us, Mr. Speaker, that it is his intention to introduce legislative changes dealing specifically with blood sampling and impaired driving in the very near future. I wish there could be a date upon that introduction. I am of the opinion that it would be wise to wait until we gather all of the information that is necessary so that we can proceed together to draft legislation dealing with this matter. One might say that this afternoon is the time to do this. I think perhaps we would get better legislation if it were indeed discussed in committee. I for one would be more than happy to take part in such discussions.
Let me address myself, Mr. Speaker, to some recent developments which have occurred at the provincial level regarding blood sampling. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West, mentioned that to date some Provinces have introduced bills dealing with blood sampling. He mentioned Manitoba, British Columbia and 1 believe Saskatchewan. In the case of British Columbia, the provisions have been proclaimed and will come into force in a matter of a few weeks. 1 would like to quote directly from Section 220.2 of Bill 69 which provides that, where a peace officer on reasonable and probable grounds believes that a person has:
(a)	within the preceding two hours driven a motor vehicle or had the care and control of a motor vehicle on a highway or industrial road, and
(b)	consumed alcohol
he may require that a person provide a blood sample.
Section 220.3(1) provides that a person who without reasonable excuse fails or refuses to comply with a demand commits an offence.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West, suggested that one of his lawyer friends would like to add certain fines to that. 1 believe that that could possibly be a good way to proceed.
Section 220.2(2) states that where a person is incapable due to physical or mental trauma of comprehending the nature of a demand, a blood sample may be taken from that person without a demand being made. I agree with that. I agree that at the very least that should be done.
Public outcry in Saskatchewan has been sustained since the major traffic disaster at Webb in the summer of 1980 in which 22 lives were lost and breath samples could not be demanded from the dirver because of his physical condition. Bill 81 with the amendments to the Vehicle Act received third reading and Royal Assent by the Legislative Assembly of Saskatchewan on June 2, 1983. In many ways that law is the same as the law of British Columbia.
Section 168(3) makes provision for a case where a peace officer, on reasonable and probable grounds, believes that a person has consumed alcohol or drugs. The drugs that are being used today are not an entirely new phenomenon and perhaps this should be included in the proposed legislation. It also provides that where the officer believes that a person within the preceding two hours has driven or had the care and control of a motor vehicle and is incapable of providing a
sample of his breath, the peace officer may, subject to Subsection (4), by demand made to that person, require him or her to provide sufficient sample of blood that, in the opinion of the person taking the sample, is necessary to enable a proper analysis to be made to determine the proportion, if any, of alcohol and/or drugs in the blood and to accompany the peace officer for the purpose of enabling the sample to be taken.
Section 168(4) states that where a person is, in the opinion of the peace officer, incapable of understanding the nature of a demand for a sample of his blood, the peace officer may cause a sample of his blood to be taken without a demand. I agree with that.
Section 168(5) makes it an offence for any person without reasonable excuse to fail to comply with a demand to provide a blood sample.
James Garner, Saskatchewan Minister of Highways and transportation, has stated that the Saskatchewan provisions would be proclaimed into force on October 1, 1983.
Both of these Bills raise questions-which could be answered if we had the information available-as to whether they are constitutional in light of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Let us look at the situation in some other countries. The Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West dealt with the law in California where I believe he said that anyone who drives on the highways there, by the mere fact of driving an automobile, consents to having a blood test.
He also referred to Australia. Each of the Australian states has a provision for a screening test of blood alcohol concentration. The purpose of this test is the same as our roadside testing provision in Section 234(1) of the Criminal Code. Persons "passing" the test are generally released from the obligation to undergo breath analysis or a blood test, whichever may be appropriate, for evidentiary purposes. Each state law in Australia contains a provision for the determination of blood alcohol concentration by the use of a breath analysing instrument. It is the primary means of ascertaining blood alcohol concentration in each Australian state and territory. The police in each state may require a person to submit to a breath analysis if it appears from the screening test that the percentage of alcohol in blood exceeds, or in some cases equals, the prescribed limit. It may also be required if a person refuses or fails to provide a sample for a screening test. Although the primary means of ascertaining blood alcohol concentration throughout Australia is by breath analysis, there is provision in each state for blood tests in certain circumstances.
The Hon. Member did not mention that in the United Kingdom recent amendments were made as a result of the recommendations in the Blennerhassett Report in April, 1976. Breath tests are now accepted for evidentiary purposes as the principal means of determining the blood alcohol concentration of drivers. Prior to the amendments, breath samples could be required solely in connection with a preliminary screening
September 14, 1983

test; only the results of blood or urine analysis could be adduced as an evidentiary sample.
Enforcement of this legislation proved difficult, particularly as it related to the screening tests. Blood or urine tests of many accused were clearly over the limit, yet legislative loopholes allowed them to continue to drive undeterred. Changes sought effective enforcement and the whittling down of technical defences. The power of the police to require a breath test was extended to cover persons who had been in charge of a motor vehicle. In addition, it attacked the "hip flask"defence so that drinking after an accident could not be used to disguise impairment before the accident. It is almost incomprehensible to me in this day and age that people, having been in an accident where other individuals were maimed or killed, would have the effrontery or would be so heartless as to drink more alcohol so that it could not be proven whether they were drunk before or after the accident.
Their Road Traffic Act of 1972, as amended, makes provision for a constable to demand that a person submit to a breath, blood or urine test in addition to a preliminary breath screening test. Section 8(1) of the legislation provides that, in the course of an investigation whether a person has committed an offence under section 5, which is driving, attempting to drive or being in charge while under the influence of drink or drugs, or section 6, which is driving, attempting to drive, or being in charge with blood alcohol concentration above the prescribed limit, that is .08, a constable may require him to provide two specimens of breath for analysis by means of an appropriate device, or to provide a specimen of blood or urine for laboratory test.
The amendments permit the result of a breath test to be used for evidentiary purposes. When the roadside screening test proves positive, a second breath test, rather than a blood or urine sample, is the normal means of providing evidence at the police station. This change was supported by medical experts who proposed that blood or urine sampling should be replaced by breath analysis. The new breath-testing provisions enable police officers to determine the alcohol content of blood within minutes and removes the need to send for doctors to administer blood tests.
Section 8(4) of that legislation states that if the provision of a specimen other than a specimen of breath may be required, the question whether it is to be a specimen of blood or urine shall be decided by the constable, except that if a medical practitioner is of the opinion that for medical purposes a specimen of blood cannot or should not be taken, it shall be a specimen of urine. Section 8(7) provides that a person who, without reasonable excuse, fails to provide a specimen when required to do so, is guilty of an offence.
Section 8(8) provides that, on requiring any person to provide a specimen, a constable must warn him that failure to provide it may render him liable to imprisonment, a fine, and disqualification. That is precisely what the Hon. Member's lawyer friend said might be done. If the constable fails to give the warning, the court may direct an acquittal or dismiss the charge, the issue being whether prejudice had resulted from
Blood Samples
failure to give a warning. Some of our friends claim that individual rights are being trampled upon, but at least they have access to the courts which is more than the victims of the accident have.
The subsection obviously contemplates that a person may be convicted though no warning is given, so the warning cannot be a requirement of the offence. However, if a person is charged with failing to provide a specimen, absence of a warning is relevant to the issue of reasonable excuse.
Section 9 gives additional protection to hospitalized persons. It provides that, while a person is at hospital as a patient, he shall not be required to provide a specimen of breath for a breath test or to provide a specimen for a laboratory test unless the medical practitioner in immediate charge has been notified and that it shall be for the provision of a specimen at the hospital. However, if the medical practitioner objects on the ground that it would be prejudicial to the proper care and treatment of the patient, the requirement shall not be made.
It seems abundantly clear, Mr. Speaker, from what has been said by my colleague and myself, that there are a number of options available regarding the acquisition of blood, and this House and the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs should have the benefit of the comparative review of blood sampling legislation which is being carried out by the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) and the officials within his Department before embarking upon proposals to amend the Criminal Code in this area.
It seems that Hon. Members on the other side are taken with the fact that we are taking time to discuss the Bill as it is now. I suggest to them that the proper place for discussion of this Bill and the principle of this Bill-and I say this with all respect to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West-could best be done in committee. If it does go to committee I, for one, will gladly support it there.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by expressing my sympathy, through the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman), to the Steward family who so tragically lost their son through impaired driving. The slaughter on our highways by drunk drivers is a terrible thing and our laws are certainly not tough enough. I, like many Canadians, have lost a close family member through drunk driving. A cousin of mine at the age of 17, on his high school graduation, was killed in an accident caused by drunk driving, so I know very personally the tragedy which this causes to families.
We do know some of the very specific technical problems which result because of the loopholes in our current laws. There are drivers who are unconscious after an accident and avoid a breathalyzer test which would end up in their being convicted. This reduces the chance of obtaining convictions. There are also people who seek to evade criminal responsibility by faking unconsciousness. This is another loophole with which we have to deal. Our laws do need considerable revision. I take

September 14, 1983
Blood Samples
this problem very, very seriously and 1 believe we do have to address some of the objections which have been raised by people who take a different approach. 1 do not agree with them all, as I will point out; however, I feel their objections have to be considered. Civil liberties associations, for example, have raised protests on grounds of self-incrimination through blood analysis. 1 do not accept this objection because I feel that driving is a privilege not a right. When one goes to get a driver's licence one does not receive the right to drive under all circumstances. You accept certain obligations and I believe one of them is, obviously, not to drink. Another is to subject yourself to laws which ensure that drunk drivers are kept off the highways.
That being said, it does not mean that a blood test is the best means of dealing with the problem which we have to face. There is a possibility of using different kinds of equipment, for example, new equipment which will enable a breathalyzer test to be taken from unconscious persons. There is a possibility that saliva and urine samples can be used to give adequate information. Certainly, if these means can be effectively developed, and there are technical questions about them, they would be a better means of dealing with the question than using blood samples. We have to consider the problems, for example, of hemophiliacs and of infection caused by taking blood samples. We do not want to add to the list of victims in our search for a solution.
I would agree, then, with the intent and the spirit of this Bill. However, to give it second reading as it now stands would be to give agreement in principle to a particular method of control, that is, with blood tests, and that would be to prejudge the technical question as to what is the best method of obtaining the necessary information. Blood tests may be the answer, and if that is shown I would be quite willing to support compulsory blood tests in those cases. 1 would agree, then, to reference of the subject matter to committee, but not the Bill itself. I believe this would be an effective thing to do.
Further, Mr. Speaker, I would like to argue that we need to take a more comprehensive approach to this problem. The Hon. Member's Bill deals with obtaining a conviction after the fact. Of course, we want justice to be done, but surely the more important problem is to get drunk drivers off the roads. We do have laws now. We do have punishments, although they are not tough enough. But there are other things we can do to see that the punishments we mete out are successful. Something we could be doing, for example, on conviction for impaired driving, would be to impound the motor vehicle, not just take away the licence. We have the problem of people who are convicted once and who, therefore, are identified as problem drivers, as drunk drivers, but they continue to go out and do it again.
There are other means which we really must be considering in dealing with the actual problem of getting impaired drivers off the road. To do that, Mr. Speaker, we need a whole array of amendments, not just this Bill. 1 do have some concrete proposals to make. 1 am studying this problem and I feel we must address it in a very serious way.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would support reference of the subject matter to committee, not the actual Bill itself. In the alternative, I look forward to dealing with it when the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) brings in his amendments which will, of course, be referred to committee. He has promised amendments to the Criminal Code this fall on impaired driving.
