Mr. Speaker, I too salute the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman). I believe this is a Bill which is doing all Canadians a service and I feel we should all be very grateful to him for bringing it here today. The Hon. Member referred to some statistics, Mr. Speaker, but I do not believe he mentioned the figure of 18,000 Canadians killed by drunk drivers in the previous six years. Another figure is that 50 per cent of automobile accidents which occur involve a degree of liquor. The Hon. Member might well have indicated that the OECD has pointed out that Canada has the second highest fatality rate of the 24 member countries. We are exceeded only by France in that regard. The record in Canada is absolutely deplorable.
The Hon. Member gave us the case of the Steward family. May I very quickly mention a case of a constituent in an adjacent riding to mine whose daughter, aged 22, was riding in a vehicle on a divided highway. A car came down the wrong side of the divided highway and there was a head-on collision which killed this girl. The driver of the other vehicle was ultimately charged with impaired driving. The tragedy was that the girl's body was taken away for autopsy. This mother had no rights whatsoever with respect to her daughter's body. The man driving his car down the wrong side of the divided highway was not required to take a breathalyzer test.
Numerous speakers have referred to that type of situation and it seems to me this case, like the one mentioned by the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West, underlines dramatically what is wrong with the law at present. I speak as somebody who has been involved with impaired driving cases, both as a Crown attorney and as defence counsel, on many, many occasions.
Up to 1976, Sir, we had essentially just the impaired driving section. The problem with that was that once 1976 came along and we brought in the breathalyzer sections, some, and to be fair not all, of the judges took the view that the impaired driving section had in effect become a "dead letter". There have been cases, I think it is fair to say, where people who have been falling down drunk have been found not to be impaired. Therefore, all of the problems have fallen back on the breathalyzer sections. As has been pointed out here today, those sections are inadequate because you simply get up after an accident and say you are sick or you banged your head. Without plugging this loophole the law will remain grossly defective, so I submit it is high time we did so.
Many references have been made to legislation in Saskatchewan, British Columbia, Ontario, Manitoba and Alberta. I
September 14, 1983

quote from the Toronto Star of August 26, where we have the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) reported as saying:
Some people are against it because they think it is an unwarranted interference with the human persons. But it's the only way we have, when a person is unconscious or perhaps feigning unconsciousness to avoid a (breath-analysis) test, of actually getting a reading of the blood-alcohol level.
He also indicated that he favours mandatory blood tests for drivers who refuse or are unable to give breath samples.
The question I would put to my good friend, the Hon. Member for Welland (Mr. Parent), is: Why is it that all of the information is not in? This Bill can, of course, be amended in committee, so why can it not be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, which 1 remind him has nothing to do, at the moment at least. There is no reason why it could not take this reference, presumably starting next Tuesday; no reason why the matter could not be considered by them.
What is more important than this matter of impaired driving, in particular the defects in the present legislation? The Minister told us that we must waif for the department to study the matter. Sir, the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West has been studying this matter for six years and there is probably not a Member in this House who has not had a victim of impaired driving come and see him or her. I submit that the matter has been studied to death and it is time to do something rather than continue to talk about it. This is absolutely crucial to people in all parts of Canada, to groups like Parents Against Impaired Drivers, MADD and many other organizations which have been formed recently because of the slaughter of Canadians as a result of impaired driving.
If the figure is correct, 64 per cent of Canadians think Parliament is unimportant. We can do no greater service for Canadians as a whole, and for the victims of impaired driving in particular, by actually doing something instead of talking and talking and talking about this problem.
So without further ado, Sir, bearing in mind that if someone gets up on the Liberal side after I am finished, knowing the time available, and talks this Bill out, then I think they will be doing a disservice to their fellow citizens, and bearing in mind the comments of the Hon. Member for Welland that we can refer the subject matter of the Bill to the committee, I therefore move:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
Bill C-625, an Act to amend the Criminal Code, be not now read a second time but that the order be discharged, the Bill withdrawn and the subject matter thereof referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
I urge Members opposite, in particular the person who has been assigned to get up and talk the Bill out, to reflect on what they are doing and to refer the subject matter to the committee. They have nothing to lose, Mr. Speaker, and the Canadian people have everything to gain if they will do this on behalf of their fellow citizens.

May I suggest through you, Mr. Speaker, that with respect to the motion which has been made, for all of those reasons which I know can or might be supported by Members on all sides of the House, I and many other Members of this chamber have been involved in another Private Member's Bill which was sent to a committee which 1 had the privilege of chairing. I refer to the Hon. Member who sponsored Bill C-653, the Farmers and Creditors Arrangements Act, which has the declared support of all Members of this House but which has given an enormous task to the committee because in fact we did not have the opportunity or the benefit of having a ministry do the kind of work-up that is done on all of these Bills in a totally non-partisan manner in order that we can reflect properly and carefully before we come up with legislation.
I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that all of us could emotionally support the urgent and pressing nature of the arguments which have been made by the Hon. Members who preceded me. But I would prefer, having had the kind of experience to which I allude, to have the benefit of all possible examination and work-up of legislation in advance of our giving it to committee as opposed to tying up Members almost ad infinitum in trying to do the kind of work done behind the scenes for us.
In addition, I might try to add a few words with respect to the comments made by my friend, the Hon. Member for Welland (Mr. Parent). He started to point out some of the difficulties in which we might find ourselves were we to proceed too quickly. Might I suggest that as far back as 1952 the United States Supreme Court, when dealing with the case of Rochin v. California, indicated that a search of a suspect's stomach for concealed narcotics by forcing an emetic agent down his throat, causing him to regurgitate, violated the due process clause of the fourteenth amendment. The court likened the search to a coerced confession, focusing on the police brutality evident in the search. The opinion cast doubt on the validity of any unconsented search extending below the surface of the body.
Because that happened in the U.S., Mr. Speaker, it can obviously have little authority, other than persuasive, in Canada. But it does commence to point out that in fact there

September 14, 1983
Blood Samples
may be different ways and means of achieving the ends which the Hon. Member who commendably brought this Bill forward sought to achieve.
The State of New York passed the first implied consent statute in 1953. It was conceived as a means of facilitating the cause of chemical evidence in driving while intoxicated prosecutions and, at the same time, avoiding any constitutional limitation that might apply to the tests. The statute provided that anyone driving a motor vehicle in New York was deemed to have consented to a chemical test for intoxication at the direction of any police officer who had reasonable and probable cause to believe that the driver had been or was intoxicated. There was no requirement for arrest, and in the event that the driver refused to submit, his driving privilege would be revoked.
The new law tested in New York Supreme Court the following year in Schutt v. MacDuff. The facts were straightforward. The New York Commissioner of Motor Vehicles revoked the plaintiffs licence when he refused to submit to a blood test requested by a police officer following the arrest. After his acquittal on the drunk driving charge, the plaintiff brought an action challenging the revocation of his licence and the validity of the implied consent statute on four grounds: in the first instance, that it violated his right against self-incrimination; in the second, that it violated his right against unreasonable search and seizure; third, that it violated his right to due process of law; and finally, that it violated his right to equal protection. The last ground was rejected without hesitation, but the court held that the implied consent law did not infringe the plaintiffs privilege against self-incrimination. The court agreed with the legislature that the privilege or qualified right to drive could be conditioned upon waiver of the right against self-incrimination.
Since the statute permited the suspect to refuse testing, he could choose either to waive his privilege against self-incrimination or forfeit that privilege to continue driving in New York. Concerning the waiver by a person who is presumably drunk, the court held that the right against self-incrimination was inapplicable because the chemical evidence was non-testimonial.
The court further rejected the plaintiffs contention that the test constituted an unreasonable search under the fourth amendment. Since the officer had arrested him before directing the test, the search administered through the test would be reasonable as incidental to lawful arrest. The court further reasoned that any search conducted under the statute would be a consensual search because it permitted the driver to refuse. The ability to refuse obviated the need to inquire whether the test would be administered without actual consent.
The court did, however, uphold the plaintiffs claim that his driver's licence had been revoked without due process of law
and found the statute to be unconstitutional on that ground. The finding of unconstitutionality rested, in effect, on two defects in the legislation; first, that it lacked the requirement that a person be under lawful arrest at the time he refused the test; and, second, that it lacked any provision for a hearing on the grounds for revocation.
The defects cited by the court were subsequently remedied and the following year the New York Supreme Court upheld the statute in Anderson v. MacDuff.
In 1954, the United States Supreme Court, in Breithaupt v. Abraham, held that a blood test conducted on an unconscious driver did not violate the due process clause of the fourteenth amendment despite the suspect's lack of consent. The court distinguished the stomach search in Rochin by noting that a blood test was a minor intrusion into the body to which many people voluntarily subjected themselves each day. Unlike the search in Rochin, the blood test was not brutal and offensive and did not constitute conduct that shocks the conscience. On the authority of Breithaupt, chemical tests were thought to be permissible as long as police did not use excessive force in administering them. Both those cases, Rochin and Breithaupt, were decided before the court held that the fourth and fifth amendments were applicable in respect of state proceedings. The court clarified the fourth and fifth amendment issues in Schmerber v. California in 1966, which is now the leading U.S. constitutional authority on chemical tests for intoxication.
